_comment: Ported from macolima/config/claude-settings.json. Restricts Claude Code's Bash/Read tools ONLY. Interactive zsh is unrestricted — use it to pip/uv/npm install, clone, push, etc. during planning, then hand off to Claude with this permission profile in force. Paths adapted for root-in-container (rootless Docker userns=host).
_env_comment: DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER/DISABLE_UPDATES: Claude Code's self-updater runs a plain `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, which this image's npm allow-scripts allowlist blocks — the postinstall (node install.cjs, which fetches the platform-native binary) is skipped, leaving `claude --version` = 'native binary not installed' for EVERY process in the shared global install. Manifested as multiple-VS-Code-attach breaking claude, but a single auto-update is enough. Claude Code is baked at image build time (Dockerfile, with --allow-scripts) and bumped only via `scripts/profile.sh build --refresh-ai`; the runtime updater must stay off. Also set as OS env in the Dockerfile as belt-and-suspenders.

sandbox._comment: Disabled: Claude Code's bwrap sandbox needs unprivileged user namespaces, which our seccomp filter blocks. The container itself is the security boundary (cap_drop ALL + seccomp + internal network + Squid allowlist). Sub-blocks preserved inert so the file is portable.

permissions._comment: Plan interactively (you drive the shell, install deps), execute autonomously (tight denies, Anthropic-only egress through Squid). acceptEdits lets Claude freely edit code but still prompts for Bash not on the allow list. The REAL boundary is the egress proxy (domain allowlist) + seccomp (no user namespaces) + cap_drop + rootless userns; this deny list is defense-in-depth and surface-reducing, not the boundary itself. Claude Code's Bash matcher keys off the command prefix, so denies here can be routed around by wrapper commands (env, xargs, find -exec, make targets, language interpreters running local scripts). We deny the obvious routes; the proxy catches anything that makes it through.
permissions._myclickup_note: The 17 myclickup entries in `allow` are READS ONLY, deliberately. Surface AS OF 0.6.0, derived from the CLI's own parser on 2026-08-15 and never transcribed between documents: 28 commands, 17 read and 11 write. Deriving it is the rule, not a nicety — the previous version of this note said '19 commands: 13 read, 6 writes', a count that was copied across a repo boundary in prose and was 9 commands stale by 0.6.0. The 11 writes (create/update/set-status/claim/comment/tag/untag/depend/undepend/move/append-description) are absent from `allow` AND named in `ask` — and the second half is load-bearing, because ABSENCE ALONE DOES NOT PRODUCE A PROMPT. Verified 2026-08-15 in a live container: `myclickup --help`, `myclickup create --help` and a bare `myclickup create` are on neither list, and all three ran unprompted, reported as `Allowed by auto mode classifier`. Under defaultMode:auto an unlisted command is handed to a classifier whose behaviour is specified nowhere in this file, is pinned by no test in this repo, and can change under a Claude Code upgrade. An earlier form of this note claimed the writes `are absent so they hit the defaultMode:auto prompt every time` — that described a mechanism which is not the operative one, and it was written the same day without being tested. `ask` states the intent as a RULE instead of inferring it from a gap, and was itself proven to prompt before this sentence was written (see `_ask_note`). `ask` rather than `deny` for the writes because deny is absolute: it would remove the ability to approve a write interactively at all, which is a workflow this sandbox deliberately keeps (plan interactively, execute autonomously). `Bash(myclickup:*)` would have covered all 28 and was rejected — --dry-run is opt-in and therefore not a gate. No allowed entry is a prefix of a write, RE-VERIFIED against 0.6.0's surface: `comments` (allowed; reads a task's comments) cannot match `comment <id> …`; `Bash(myclickup status:*)` over-matches `statuses …` but NOT `set-status`, which is a different prefix; `Bash(myclickup task:*)` over-matching `tasks …` is harmless, both are reads. The five writes 0.6.0 added since this list was authored (set-status, depend, undepend, move, append-description) therefore all arrive prompting — the bump permitted nothing silently. `workspaces`/`query`/`subtasks` were added 2026-08-15 by owner decision (work/0016 close-out §5): all three are reads, none is a prefix of any write, and the deny guards are untouched. `workspaces` enumerates every workspace the single token sees — not a new capability, since `whoami` and `accounts` were already allowed, but it is now unprompted. The two deny entries are forward guards: no command deletes an OBJECT today — 0.6.0 issues two HTTP DELETEs, `untag` (removes a label) and `undepend` (removes a dependency edge), neither of which destroys an object — and the point is that a future version adding one arrives DENIED rather than silently newly-permitted. Deny is the one layer proven to outrank the classifier: verified 2026-08-15 that `myclickup delete --help` was blocked before execution, and blocked even when the agent wrapped it as `myclickup delete --help 2>&1 | head -30` — a trailing pipe does not change the prefix. That is why `delete`/`rm` stay in deny while the 11 real writes go to `ask`. The allow list is reviewed at paste time, the CLI is upgraded by image rebuild, and those two events are months apart. DEPLOYMENT: seeding is create-only (profile.sh ensure_state, init-profile-state.sh), so an edit here reaches NO running profile until `scripts/profile.sh <profile> reset-settings` is run per profile and claude is restarted in that container. This block sat in the template but in none of the three profiles from 2026-08-10 to 2026-08-15 for exactly that reason; verify does not check it. Confirm a template edit landed by diffing the live file, never by trusting the copy. Accepted residual, same as the wrapper-routing caveat above: `Bash(just:*)` and `Bash(make:*)` are allowed, so a workspace recipe wrapping a write runs unprompted.
permissions._myclickup_dryrun_note: `Bash(myclickup --dry-run:*)` is the inert form of the eleven writes (0.6.0 — see the count-derivation rule in the note above), and what makes a reads-only list workable rather than merely restrictive. myclickup >= 0.2.0 accepts --dry-run BEFORE the subcommand (its ADR-0007) precisely so a prefix pattern can match it — the trailing form is indistinguishable from a live write to a prefix matcher. It prints the RESOLVED request, which matters because the permission prompt shows argv: only the dry-run reveals that --list "Team/Build/Action Items" became a list ID and --due 2026-09-01 became epoch-ms. It widens nothing (the reads are already allowed individually), and verified 2026-08-10 in a throwaway container that a dry-run needs no CLICKUP_TOKEN at all — so it is inert even before auth exists.
permissions._acceptEdits_note: auto prompts on Bash not on the allow list and on tool calls that are not Read/Glob/Grep. Combined with the /workspace bind mount this means the agent can still autonomously rewrite host-visible files when you approve. To skip per-edit confirmation, change defaultMode to acceptEdits.
permissions._ask_note: `ask` forces a confirmation prompt as an explicit RULE, and that it outranks the classifier is VERIFIED, not assumed — by differential test on 2026-08-15: `myclickup create --help` ran UNPROMPTED with no ask rule present (reported as `Allowed by auto mode classifier`) and PROMPTED with this rule present. Same command, same classifier, same inert --help output; the rule was the only variable. That is the whole point: under defaultMode:auto a command on neither `allow` nor `deny` is decided by a classifier, not prompted by default (see the myclickup note above for the 2026-08-15 evidence). Every myclickup write is named here so the reads-only design is enforced rather than assumed. These patterns match the write subcommand in FIRST position only, so they do not shadow `Bash(myclickup --dry-run:*)`: `myclickup --dry-run create …` still matches the allow entry and stays inert, while `myclickup create …` lands here. Adding a write to myclickup means adding a line here — the allow list alone does not hold the line.

_hooks_comment: PreToolUse enforcement upstream of tool dispatch. The matcher-level permissions.deny list is prefix-on-tokens and cannot see destructive flags (find -delete, dd of=, etc.) or path targets (Edit to /usr/local/lib/claude-hooks/... or settings.json). The hook script handles both via regex on the full envelope. Script is baked into the image at /usr/local/lib/claude-hooks/deny-destructive.sh; the Bash/Edit tamper rules are the only enforcement layer on the script itself (agent runs as root in this repo, so the kernel write-protect macolima relies on does not apply). See docs/deny-destructive-hook-plan.md.
